prompt: A centrifugal pump's steel drive shaft fractured at the keyway after 14 months in service. The maintenance lead believes it was an overload: the impeller jammed on debris once last month. Two other explanations are on the table: fatigue from bending caused by shaft misalignment, and a material defect in this batch. The fleet has 12 identical pumps from the same installer. The plant manager wants to decide this week whether to replace all 12 shafts with a higher-strength alloy (40,000 USD, 3-week lead time). You can do one investigation step before that decision. Options: (a) re-run the static overload calculation for a jam, (b) fractographic examination of the fracture surface (800 USD, 2 days), (c) hardness and chemistry tests of the shaft material (1,500 USD, 1 week), (d) install vibration monitoring on all pumps (6,000 USD, 2 weeks). Which step do you take, why, and what would each possible result mean for the decision? What do you recommend for the other 11 pumps meanwhile?

key.text: Chooses (b) fractography as the one step, because its result distinguishes among the explanations rather than testing only one.

States what at least two of the three explanations predict on the fracture surface, e.g. beach marks or ratchet marks from a stress raiser for fatigue, a rough fibrous or sheared single-event surface for overload, an inclusion or defect at the origin for material.

Notes that a higher-strength alloy may not fix a fatigue failure at a keyway (stress concentration or misalignment drives it; higher-strength steels can be more notch-sensitive), so the 40,000 USD fix could leave the cause in place.
Does not commit to the fleet-wide alloy replacement before the discriminating result is in; ties the decision to the result.

Treats the other 11 pumps as possibly sharing the cause (same installer, same batch) and proposes a cheap interim check or protection for them, such as an alignment check, keyway inspection, or jam protection.

prompt: Our web service runs two application replicas behind a load balancer in one cloud region. Both replicas read their configuration at startup and on change from one shared configuration store. Deploys roll out to both replicas at the same moment. The database is a primary with one streaming replica in the same availability zone. Nightly backups go to object storage; nobody has ever restored one. Outages cost us roughly 20,000 USD per hour and lost orders cannot be recovered. The team says: we have redundancy everywhere. With one engineer-week of effort, what is our biggest reliability risk, and what should we do first? Rank your top three actions.

key.text: Identifies simultaneous deploys to both replicas as a common cause that defeats the app redundancy, and proposes staged, canary, or one-at-a-time rollout.
Identifies the shared configuration store as a single point or common cause for both replicas.
Identifies the database primary and replica in the same zone (and the single region) as a shared-cause risk.
Identifies never-restored backups as a latent failure, given unrecoverable lost orders.
Ranks a real restore test (or equivalent recovery drill) among the top three actions.
Keeps the top three actions within roughly one engineer-week, deferring larger moves such as multi-region.

prompt: An autoscaler reads average CPU across instances every 60 seconds and sets the instance count to current_count * (cpu / 60), aiming for 60 percent CPU. A new instance takes about 4 minutes to boot and start taking traffic, and until then it is counted in current_count but carries no load. With steady traffic, the instance count swings between about 8 and 30 every 15 to 20 minutes. A teammate proposes reading CPU every 15 seconds instead of 60 so the autoscaler reacts faster. Evaluate the proposal and recommend what to change. Say how you would check that your change worked.

key.text: Concludes that reading every 15 seconds with the same full proportional correction will not fix the swing and is likely to make it worse.
Identifies the roughly 4-minute delay between a scaling action and its effect on CPU as the cause of the oscillation.

Identifies that the measured state misrepresents the system (booting instances counted but carrying no load, so average CPU and current_count mislead), and proposes accounting for in-flight capacity or measuring only ready instances.
Proposes correcting less per step (damping, step limits, smaller fraction of the error) and/or waiting at least one boot delay (cooldown) before the next decision.
Proposes a concrete check of the change: a replay or simulation, or a controlled step in load, watching whether the count settles and in how many swings.

prompt: We ran a two-week A/B test of a new onboarding flow with users randomly assigned to each arm. Conversion: new flow 12.4 percent, old flow 11.8 percent, about 4,000 users per arm. In the second week a pricing change launched for all users. Company revenue rose 9 percent in the quarter. The product manager wants to (1) ship the new flow to everyone and (2) tell leadership the new flow drove the revenue rise. The new flow costs nothing extra to run, and either flow can be switched back in a day. What do you advise on each point, what exactly can we claim, and is more data worth collecting before shipping?

key.text: States that the 0.6-point difference is not distinguishable from noise at this sample size (z about 0.8, or a 95 percent interval of roughly -0.8 to +2.0 points, or equivalent), without inventing a precision the data does not support.
Refuses to attribute the quarterly revenue rise to the new flow, naming the pricing change and the small, uncertain effect as reasons.
Notes that random assignment protects the A/B comparison itself from the pricing change (both arms saw it), while the revenue claim has no such protection.

Ties the decision about more data to whether it could change the ship decision: since shipping is cheap and reversible, shipping (or continuing to collect data while shipped) is reasonable without a long further test, unless there is a reason to believe the new flow is worse.
Gives an accurate statement of what can be claimed, such as: no detectable difference; the result is consistent with a small gain or a small loss.
